faq.q: Why do frogs have such long legs?
faq.a: Longer legs push against the ground for longer during take-off, so the frog leaves faster and travels farther. Thanks to extra-long ankle bones, a frog's back legs are often longer than its body.
asks: Why are frog legs so big?

faq.q: How does a frog's catapult work?
faq.a: The calf muscle contracts while the ankle is held, stretching the tendon and storing energy. When the ankle releases, the tendon recoils very fast, adding power to the jump, like letting go of a stretched bow.
asks: How do frogs jump so powerfully?

faq.q: How far can a frog jump?
faq.a: Many frogs jump over ten times their body length. At the Calaveras County jumping frog contest in California, a bullfrog covered 6.55 metres in three jumps in 1986.
asks: What is the frog jumping record?

faq.q: How does a frog land safely?
faq.a: Frogs swing their front legs forward and land on their arms and chest, which bend to soak up the impact. Tree frogs often grab a branch or leaf with sticky toe pads.
asks: Do frogs land on their feet?
Why don't frogs get hurt landing?

faq.a: Most toads have shorter back legs and make short hops or walk. Their bodies are built more for walking and burrowing than for long leaps.
asks: Why do toads hop instead of jump?

facts: A frog's back leg has an extra segment because two ankle bones are elongated.
Cuban tree frogs use a tendon catapult that releases stored energy at take-off (Astley and Roberts, 2012).
The Calaveras County jumping frog record, set in 1986, is 6.55 metres in three jumps.
